source.title_on_document: AI-Generated Email Drafts Shift Culturally Distinctive Communication Styles in Professional Email

supplement.where: Appendices A-H are included on PDF pp. 11-16. Separately, p. 8, Table 3 refers to supplemental material containing full participant example emails; that material is not included and no location is supplied.
supplement.holds: Included appendices provide the power analysis, participant demographics, counterbalancing schedule, scenario and draft selection, AI draft texts, linguistic-marker definitions, survey questions, and draft preferences. The separately mentioned supplement contains full participant example emails, rather than additional effect estimates identified in the main text.

paper_design_summary: One online study analyzed 175 full-time employed Prolific participants (89 American and 86 Japanese), each writing workplace emails without AI first and then with low-context and high-context AI drafts. Scenario order followed a Latin square and AI draft order was counterbalanced, but the paper does not state random assignment to the orders; cultural group was a between-person factor. The authors scored linguistic markers in the submitted emails and overlap with the supplied AI drafts, studying communication-style shifts rather than directly measuring creativity or similarity between different writers' outputs.

studies.label: Online workplace-email study with a fixed no-AI baseline and counterbalanced AI drafts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every participant completed No-AI as Task 1, then AI Low-Context Draft and AI High-Context Draft in Tasks 2 and 3. Scenario types were rotated using a Latin square and AI draft order was independently counterbalanced, producing six combinations per cultural group. Allocation of people to these combinations is not described as random or explicitly non-random. Thus the no-AI comparison is fixed before/after, while randomization of the AI-configuration comparison remains unstated.
assignment.quote: the order of the two AI draft types (Low-Context vs. High-Context) across Tasks 2 and 3 was independently counterbalanced (Conditions A and B), yielding six unique combinations for each culture (see Appendix C).
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.2 Design and Procedure; p. 12, Appendix C; p. 13, Table 5.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 3, Section 3 Method (preregistered before data collection); p. 2, Preregistration and Dataset (https://aspredicted.org/2jy53q.pdf). The linked public AsPredicted preregistration was also read in memory as HTML; item 1 confirms that no data had been collected and item 4 describes counterbalancing without stating random allocation.

arms.name: No-AI
arms.description: Task 1: wrote from scratch using a plain email interface. The 175 analyzed people also appear in each AI condition; these are repeated conditions, not separate groups. PDF p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 6, Section 4.1 and Figure 4; p. 7, Figure 5.

arms.name: AI Low-Context Draft
arms.description: One of Tasks 2 and 3: could request a pre-generated low-context draft and edit it freely or write from scratch. The analysis retained participants who generated drafts in both AI conditions. PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.2-3.5; p. 7, Figure 5.

arms.name: AI High-Context Draft
arms.description: The other of Tasks 2 and 3: could request a pre-generated high-context draft and edit it freely or write from scratch. The same participants contributed to all conditions. PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.2-3.5; p. 7, Figure 5.

participants.exclusions: Participants without full-time employment were screened out at eligibility (number not stated). Only participants who generated an AI draft in both AI conditions were retained. Section 3.5 lists 87 Japanese and 90 American participants meeting this condition, then states that one Japanese and one American participant were excluded because their submitted emails did not match the assigned scenario. The final analysis includes 175 people (86 Japanese, 89 American). Section 3.5 reports 257 recruited, whereas Section 4 uses a draft-generation denominator of 228; the paper does not reconcile these counts, and neither is treated as a randomized count. PDF p. 5, Sections 3.5 and 4; p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 7, Figure 5; p. 13, Table 4.
participants.who: Full-time employed adults recruited through Prolific in the United States and Japan; the main analysis includes 89 American and 86 Japanese participants who generated drafts in both AI conditions and passed the scenario-relevance check. Section 3.5 reports 257 recruited, whereas Section 4 reports a draft-generation denominator of 228 without reconciling the difference; neither is treated as a randomized count. The final analysis count of 175 is explicitly confirmed in Figure 5 and Appendix H.
participants.quote: We answer these questions with a controlled, preregistered experiment involving 175 full-time Japanese and American employed adults (86 Japanese, 89 American).
participants.locator: PDF p. 2, Introduction (quote); p. 5, Sections 3.5 and 4 (recruitment and analysis selection); p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 7, Figure 5 and Section 4.3; p. 13, Table 4; p. 15, Appendix H.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Flash
ai_tool.how_used: Participants could click Generate Draft to receive a fixed, pre-generated full email draft for the assigned scenario, then edit freely or ignore it. Everyone in the same scenario and draft condition saw identical text. Drafts were selected to maximize the high-context versus low-context style contrast and supplied in Japanese or English. PDF p. 4, Sections 3.2-3.3; pp. 12-14, Appendices D-E.

task.description: Compose three professional emails in the participant's native language to an imagined established supervisor: a favor-request, a disagreement, and a task-refusal, with a different scenario in each assistance condition. These were simulated workplace emails assessed for cultural communication style. PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 14, Table 6.

outcomes.name: Change from no-AI baseline in composite high-context communication score: human-coded indirectness and imposition-mitigation markers per 100 words
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Low-context versus high-context AI draft: adjusted LMM condition coefficient beta = -4.75, SE = 0.19, z = -25.71, p < .001. Descriptive mean changes from the no-AI baseline were M = -2.09 for low-context and M = +2.60 for high-context, in markers per 100 words. The model included a random intercept per participant. The score counts linguistic markers coded by a single bilingual coder; a higher score denotes more high-context communication, not greater creativity or greater diversity.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 4-5, Section 3.4.1 (scoring); p. 6, Section 4.2 (outcome and model); p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 5 (all reported estimates).

eligibility.reason: Core is no because emails are scored for cultural communication style and overlap with their supplied AI draft, with no qualifying creativity or between-writer similarity/diversity outcome (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.4.1-3.4.2; pp. 6-8, Sections 4.1-4.4; p. 9, Section 5; creativity-codebook.md, Sections 1, 3 and 6). The 175 analyzed people meet the sample criterion (PDF p. 7, Figure 5; p. 13, Table 4; p. 15, Appendix H). No-AI always came first; the order of the two AI conditions was counterbalanced without stated random allocation (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.2; p. 13, Table 5; linked AsPredicted preregistration at https://aspredicted.org/2jy53q.pdf, public HTML, item 4). Criterion 1 remains unclear for the AI-configuration comparison. The fixed-baseline comparison is quasi_people, but without an in-scope output outcome this study does not qualify as observational context.

one_line_finding: Among 175 analyzed participants, descriptive high-context marker scores changed by -2.09 per 100 words with low-context AI drafts and +2.60 with high-context drafts relative to the fixed no-AI baseline; the adjusted low-versus-high contrast was beta = -4.75 (SE = 0.19, p < .001; PDF p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 5).
